title: Media distortion, news framing and mediatization
headings: The original concept of media distortion Media distortion 2.0 News framing and the construction of meaning Frames in the communication process Generic frames and methodological precision From framing to mediatization The integrated contribution to analysis work in issue and risk management References
text: Media distortion, news framing and mediatization | MMP311 Skip to main content MMP311 A− A A+ Media distortion, news framing and mediatization MMP311 · Version 1.0 · Revised 19th of November, 2026 by Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) Issue, risk and crisis analysis often begins before a situation has acquired a stable definition. An event, complaint, policy proposal or public controversy may constitute an issue for one actor, a problem for another and a possible risk for a third. Analysis must therefore examine how the situation becomes relevant, which consequences are made visible, which values organise disagreement and which actors acquire the authority to define what the situation concerns. News media constitute one part of the environment under analysis. Their significance does not lie only in disseminating information. Journalistic selection and presentation affect which aspects of a situation become publicly visible, how actors and consequences are connected, and which definitions appear credible or actionable. Public communication may therefore influence the conditions under which organisations detect issues, assess problems and risks, and decide whether a response requires communication, organisational change or both. Media distortion, news framing and mediatization describe different levels of this process. Media distortion identifies techniques used to select and present information. Framing concerns how selected elements are organised into interpretations of problems, causes, responsibilities and possible responses. Mediatization concerns longer-term changes in the relationships between media and other institutions. Maintaining these distinctions makes it possible to move from close analysis of a particular text to an assessment of public relevance and, where the material permits it, institutional change. The original concept of media distortion Hernes first developed the concept of medievri in the 1970s. The original argument addressed the transition from an information-poor to an information-rich society. The institutional question was how media altered the internal functioning of other social units and the relationships among them (Hernes, 1977, p. 181). In the information-rich society, abundance created a shortage of attention and assessment time. Selection and presentation consequently became central. The original model identified sharpening, simplification, polarisation, intensification and concretisation. Sharpening makes a principal point more distinct. Simplification reduces complexity. Polarisation organises actors and positions through contrast. Intensification strengthens conflict or confrontation. Concretisation gives priority to observable events and examples over abstract relationships (Hernes, 1977, pp. 187–188). Personification was omitted from the original article and added later (Hernes, 2019, p. 30). These techniques do not necessarily indicate factual error, deliberate manipulation or poor journalism. Hernes tied them to limited capacity, assumptions about normal knowledge, democratic accessibility and the need to attract an audience (Hernes, 1977, p. 188). The analytical task is therefore to show what each operation does in the material. Sharpening may clarify an issue while narrowing the range of relevant interpretations. Concretisation may make an abstract risk understandable through a particular case while obscuring structural conditions. Personification may make responsibility visible while dire

title: Glossary
text: Glossary | MMP311 Skip to main content MMP311 Glossary Core concepts used across issue, risk and crisis analysis. Issue A matter becomes an issue when an actor makes conduct, consequences, values or responsibility relevant before the organisation has established that a problem exists. Problem A documented condition that obstructs valued outcomes or creates an expectation gap requiring investigation, clarification or change. Risk Possible future consequences considered together with uncertainty, exposure, vulnerability and what actors value. Crisis A situation that threatens valued outcomes, compresses decision time and challenges ordinary organisational capacity. Public A group that forms around a recognised consequence, shared concern or contested value. A public is not identical to a predefined target group. Framing Selection and organisation of elements into an interpretation of a problem, causes, evaluations and possible responses. Media distortion Presentational operations such as sharpening, simplification, polarisation, intensification, concretisation and personification. Mediatization Longer-term changes in relationships between media and other institutions that alter communicative conditions and organisational practices. PRK An analytical model for conditional movement among problem, risk and crisis. The model does not assume automatic escalation. SOFT A reflexive model for testing social and organisational assumptions, missing publics and blind spots in a situation analysis. FIVER A five-stage framework for understanding, identifying, evaluating, changing and responding to issues, possible problems and risks.

Start the learning path Official course description (opens in a new tab) Issue contested expectations Risk uncertainty and consequences Crisis acute pressure and response Course perspective Three analytical objects, one organisational process Issue A contested matter develops when organisational conduct, public expectations and competing interpretations no longer align. Issue management asks what the organisation must notice, understand and change. Risk Risk communication concerns possible consequences, uncertainty, values and trust. Technical assessments matter, but they do not settle how people interpret what is at stake. Crisis A crisis creates acute pressure on operations, legitimacy or both. Communication is part of the response, not an activity added after operational decisions have been made. Issues, risks and crises are related, but escalation is not inevitable. Context, decisions and learning change the movement between them. Analytical frameworks PRK, SOFT and FIVER PRK Problem, risk and crisis PRK maps movement between an emerging problem, increasing risk and crisis. The model also follows the reverse movement: crisis response can create new problems, expectations and risks. What has changed? Who defines the situation? What could develop if the organisation does not act? Explore PRK → SOFT Issues are socially interpreted SOFT widens attention beyond technical probability and consequence. It examines social conditions, opinion, framing, transparency and organisational conditions. Which voices are heard? How is the issue framed? What can the organisation explain or change? Explore SOFT → FIVER From understanding to response FIVER organises issue and risk work as a recurring process of understanding, identifying, evaluating, revising and responding. headings: Learning outcomes Hazard, risk, uncertainty and ambiguity Read for First and second modernity Manufactured and de-bounded risks Invisibility and non-knowledge Organised irresponsibility and unequal consequences Worked example Student activity Common misunderstanding Expected output Further reading and teaching context Check your understanding
text: Risk, uncertainty and the social production of relevance | MMP311 Skip to main content MMP311 A− A A+ Learning path Risk society Risk communication Issues management PRK and SOFT FIVER Crisis communication Academic writing 8 February, 09:00–15:00 Risk, uncertainty and the social production of relevance MMP311 · Version 1.1 · Revised 19th of November, 2026 by Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) Learning outcomes Distinguish hazard, risk, uncertainty and ambiguity. Explain manufactured, de-bounded and unequally distributed risk. Use non-knowledge and unknown unknowns in a case analysis. Identify who decides and who carries possible consequences. Risk is not simply a measurable property of a hazard. It is also a way of anticipating possible harm under conditions of incomplete knowledge, disagreement and unequal exposure. Hazard, risk, uncertainty and ambiguity Hazard A potential source of harm. Risk A possible development considered in relation to valued outcomes, decisions and consequences. Uncertainty Limits to what is known about probability, consequences, causal relations or future development. Ambiguity Disagreement about meaning, values, responsibility or acceptable action, even when actors share some of the same factual information. Read for Beck: de-bounding, anticipation and world risk society. Sørensen: calculability, non-knowledge and constructivist realism. Source basis. Sørensen shows that Beck’s risk concept is not equivalent to conventional calculable risk. Beck’s “new risks” combine manufactured origins with qualities associated with hazards: they may be difficult to calculate, insure, delimit and observe directly (Sørensen, 2018, pp. 6–12). First and second modernity In first modernity, industrial institutions treated uncertainty as something that could increasingly be measured, insured and controlled. Beck’s second or reflexive modernity describes a condition in which modernisation confronts the side effects of its own success. Scientific and technological development remains necessary, but also produces hazards, dependencies and non-knowledge that established institutions struggle to contain (Sørensen, 2018, pp. 7–9). Manufactured and de-bounded risks Beck’s world risk society is not defined by a simple increase in everyday danger. It is defined by risks that cross spatial, temporal and social boundaries. Beck uses ecological, financial and terrorist risks to show how consequences escape national control, unfold over long periods and make causal responsibility difficult to assign (Beck, 2002, pp. 40–45). These risks are unequally distributed. Their transnational reach does not mean that all groups or regions are exposed in the same way. Decisions and benefits may be concentrated in one place while consequences are carried elsewhere (Beck, 2002, pp. 41–42; Sørensen, 2018, pp. 13–15). Invisibility and non-knowledge Many modern risks cannot be perceived directly. Radiation, climate change and toxic exposure become visible through scientific theories, instruments and institutional practices. Sørensen describes this through Beck’s idea of “second-hand non-experience”: citizens depend on expertise to identify risks while scientific disagreement can increase rather than remove uncertainty (Sørensen, 2018, pp. 7–10). Beck distinguishes what is not yet known from “unknown unknowns”: knowledge whose absence is itself unknown when decisions are made. title: Risk communication as knowledge and trust work
headings: Learning outcomes Assessment, perception and communication Three communication situations Expertise, ethos and warranted trust Use SOFT to test the communication Worked example Student activity Common misunderstanding Expected output Check your understanding
text: Risk communication as knowledge and trust work | MMP311 Skip to main content MMP311 A− A A+ Learning path Risk society Risk communication Issues management PRK and SOFT FIVER Crisis communication Academic writing 11 February, 09:00–12:00 Risk communication as knowledge and trust work MMP311 · Version 1.1 · Revised 19th of November, 2026 by Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) Learning outcomes Distinguish risk assessment, risk perception and risk communication. Identify care, consensus and crisis communication. Assess whether trust is warranted by competence, integrity and conduct. Use SOFT to identify social and organisational blind spots. Risk communication connects assessment, public interpretation, values and practical action. It cannot be reduced to transferring expert information to a passive audience. Assessment, perception and communication Risk assessment evaluates possible harm, uncertainty and vulnerability. Risk perception concerns how actors interpret relevance, credibility, fairness and control. Risk communication is the exchange through which knowledge, uncertainty, values and possible action are made available for scrutiny and decision. Three communication situations Care communication Supports informed choices and protective action where the hazard is reasonably established. Consensus communication Addresses disagreement about decisions, values, distribution and acceptable risk. Crisis communication Supports urgent action and coordination under time pressure, uncertainty and possible harm. The situations may overlap. A crisis can contain long-standing value conflict, and care communication may fail when unequal resources make recommended action unrealistic. Expertise, ethos and warranted trust Expert knowledge enters a particular rhetorical situation. Audiences assess not only the information, but also the expert, the institution, previous conduct and the interests surrounding the claim. Trust should not be treated as an attitude that communication can manufacture. Communication supports warranted trust when competence, integrity, goodwill, uncertainty and institutional limitations are visible. Use SOFT to test the communication SOFT asks whether the communication accounts for social conditions, opinions and expectations, framing, transparency and organisational conditions. The lens helps distinguish an information deficit from a conflict about values, unequal consequences or organisational conduct. Worked example A drinking-water warning combines crisis communication with care communication. Residents need immediate protective advice, but the authority must also explain uncertainty, unequal access to alternatives and when new information will be available. Student activity Compare an expert message and a public response concerning the same risk. Identify what each treats as evidence, which uncertainty is acknowledged, which values are contested, and which recommendations assume resources that some audiences may not have. Common misunderstanding Being open about uncertainty is not the same as being vague. Useful uncertainty communication states what is known, what is not known, why the limitation matters and what will happen next. Expected output A short risk message containing known evidence, explicit uncertainty, recommended action, justification and an accessibility check. text: Issue detection and problem prevention | MMP311 Skip to main content MMP311 A− A A+ Learning path Risk society Risk communication Issues management PRK and SOFT FIVER Crisis communication Academic writing 16 February, 09:00–12:00 Issue detection and problem prevention MMP311 · Version 1.1 · Revised 19th of November, 2026 by Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) Learning outcomes Explain why an issue precedes a possible problem. Identify who makes a matter relevant and on what grounds. Separate investigation and adaptation from organisational defence. Analyse how journalistic techniques affect visibility. An issue begins when an actor makes a matter relevant by questioning conduct, consequences, values or responsibility. Early issues management examines the claim before the organisation defines the matter as a problem. Issue before problem An issue may be clarified, accommodated or resolved before it produces a problem. It becomes a problem when it creates an expectation gap, obstructs legitimate goals, harms stakeholders or places the organisation under sustained pressure to act. Early work therefore asks who points to the issue, which experience or evidence supports the claim, and what the organisation can clarify or change. Possible responses include clarification, participation, adaptation, changes in policy or practice, and a reasoned rejection of a claim. Issues management is not organisational self-defence. It is a systematic way to test whether conduct, consequences, values or responsibility require action. How an issue becomes visible Hernes’s concept of media distortion ( medievridning ) identifies accentuation, simplification, polarisation, intensification, concretisation and personification as techniques that shape attention. These techniques do not automatically create the underlying problem. They affect what becomes visible, how responsibility is attributed and how quickly an organisation must respond. Worked example A local group questions a proposed service change. The issue exists when the claim is made relevant. It becomes an organisational problem only if the proposal creates an unresolved expectation gap, material harm or sustained conflict. Student activity Select an emerging issue. State what can still be clarified before it becomes a problem. Identify the conduct or non-response that could move the issue towards risk or crisis, and propose one preventive organisational change. Common misunderstanding Media attention documents visibility, not proof that the organisation caused the issue. The underlying claim, conduct and consequences require separate evidence. Expected output A one-page issue brief identifying the claim, evidence, stakeholders, expectation gap, clarification needs and possible organisational change. Check your understanding Who defines an issue? What can prevent an issue from becoming a problem? What evidence is needed before a claim is rejected? Full-text explanation. Media distortion, framing and mediatization clarify how issues become visible and publicly relevant. Read media distortion, news framing and mediatization . text: PRK and SOFT: movement, attention and interpretation | MMP311 Skip to main content MMP311 A− A A+ Learning path Risk society Risk communication Issues management PRK and SOFT FIVER Crisis communication Academic writing 18 February, 09:00–12:00 PRK and SOFT: movement, attention and interpretation MMP311 · Version 1.1 · Revised 19th of November, 2026 by Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) Learning outcomes Use PRK without assuming automatic escalation. Recognise new issues, problems and risks created by crisis response. Use SOFT to identify blind spots in a situation analysis. Distinguish media distortion, framing, media logic and mediatization. PRK locates conditional movement between problem, risk and crisis. SOFT challenges what the first situation analysis has made visible. Issue detection before PRK An issue stands before the PRK triad. It may be clarified without becoming a problem. If the matter exposes an expectation gap, material harm or sustained conflict, it may reveal or produce a problem. A problem may create risk without becoming a crisis, while crisis response may create new problems and risks. Issue A matter made relevant by an actor Clarified or handled Dialogue, adaptation or reasoned rejection Problem Expectation gap, harm or sustained pressure Problem ↔ Risk ↔ Crisis ↺ learning and new issues Figure 1. Issue detection precedes PRK. Movement is conditional and reversible, not an inevitable escalation. SOFT as a critical lens The resource uses SOFT as the name of a teaching lens rather than as a strict letter-by-letter initialism. It tests social conditions, opinions and expectations, framing, transparency and organisational conditions. The lens asks whose exposure and knowledge are visible, which interpretation dominates, what the organisation can explain, and whether it has authority and capacity to change. Media distortion, framing, media logic and mediatization These concepts operate at different analytical levels. Media distortion concerns concrete presentation techniques. Framing concerns selection, problem definition, causal interpretation, responsibility and remedies. Media logic concerns technological, aesthetic and institutional working conditions. Mediatization concerns longer-term changes in the relationship between media and other institutions. The levels can be connected analytically, but they do not constitute a single documented causal chain. Worked example A technical disruption may be handled without public controversy. If service users experience unequal consequences, the disruption becomes a problem. Poor response may create legitimacy risk, while an acute operational breakdown may become a crisis and generate new issues. SOFT worksheet Table 1. Five fields for challenging the first situation analysis. Field Question Evidence What may be missing? Social conditions Who is exposed, excluded or dependent? Opinions and expectations What do stakeholders consider legitimate or safe? Framing How are cause, responsibility and remedies defined? Transparency What is known, unknown, withheld or difficult to explain? Organisational conditions What authority, resources and capacity for change exist? Student activity Apply PRK and SOFT to the same case. First locate the movement. Then identify what the first account misses because of social position, framing, transparency or organisational limits. text: FIVER: from understanding to response | MMP311 Skip to main content MMP311 A− A A+ Learning path Risk society Risk communication Issues management PRK and SOFT FIVER Crisis communication Academic writing 23 February, 09:00–12:00 FIVER: from understanding to response MMP311 · Version 1.1 · Revised 19th of November, 2026 by Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) Author-developed framework, first used in 2025. This English resource adapts Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) ’s Norwegian teaching text used with students at NTNU and HAW Kiel. Learning outcomes Use the five FIVER phases and fifteen work tasks. Separate strategic aims from tactical tasks. Identify organisational change before proposing communication measures. Plan evaluation and institutional learning. FIVER retains its Norwegian acronym: F orstå (frame and understand), I dentifisere (identify), V urdere (evaluate), E ndre (change) and R espondere (respond). It is a five-stage framework for understanding and handling issues, possible problems and risks before they develop into crises. Trust-building, expectation management and learning remain strategic aims throughout the process. 1. Frame and understand Map stakeholders and expectations, analyse drivers and the media environment, and establish structures for information and communication. The first stage should include communication, empathy, cooperation and cultural understanding, because these conditions affect whether the organisation is perceived as credible and responsible. Map stakeholders and their expectations. Analyse drivers, public debate and the media environment. Build structures and plans, using SOFT, FMECA, PSO or another suitable system. 2. Identify Identify issues that may develop into problems. Clarify expectation gaps, distinguish relevant signals from noise, and prioritise matters according to their possible consequences and need for follow-up. Clarify expectation gaps. Distinguish noise from relevant risk signals. Prioritise and rank issues. 3. Evaluate Assess probability, consequences, uncertainty and vulnerability. Locate causes and responsibility, examine gaps between stakeholder expectations and organisational practice, and test whether the matter has been framed too narrowly. The analysis must also establish whether the problem is communicative, organisational, financial, technical or operational. Analyse probability and consequence without treating the matrix as the whole assessment. Locate causes, responsibility and missing redundancy. Critically reassess the problem definition and examine expectation gaps. Reframing is not positive spin. 4. Change Move from analysis to action. Choose a reactive, adaptive, proactive, initiative-taking or interactive strategy. Revise plans, resources, routines, roles and organisational structures. Distinguish material, organisational, strategic and communicative change. Adjusting the narrative cannot replace material or organisational change. Select a strategy suited to the issue and the organisation. Adapt plans, resources and measures. Revise communication, roles or structures where necessary. 5. Respond Put decisions into practice. Communication must correspond with action, coordination must include relevant stakeholders and partners, and evaluation must occur during as well as after the response. text: Crisis communication as part of crisis management | MMP311 Skip to main content MMP311 A− A A+ Learning path Risk society Risk communication Issues management PRK and SOFT FIVER Crisis communication Academic writing 25 February, 09:00–12:00 Crisis communication as part of crisis management MMP311 · Version 1.1 · Revised 19th of November, 2026 by Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) Author’s adapted translation. This resource reorganises and expands selected arguments from the crisis communication chapter in Brataas, Bakken, and Fuglseth (2026), Etterpåklok på forhånd . It is not a reproduction of the published chapter. Learning outcomes Distinguish crisis information from crisis communication. Plan internal and external communication as connected work. Write an initial update under uncertainty. Prioritise stakeholders, channels and fallback channels. Evaluate communication as part of crisis management. Crisis communication is part of crisis management. Information affects safety, coordination, legitimacy and the organisation’s capacity to act. Crisis information and crisis communication Crisis information distributes verified facts and instructions. Crisis communication is broader: it connects decision-making, listening, coordination, interpretation, uncertainty and relations with affected groups. Internal communication must begin before or alongside external communication because employees, leaders and operational teams need a shared basis for action. Before, during and after Before a crisis, the organisation maps scenarios, stakeholders, responsibilities, channels and fallback systems, and practises difficult decisions. During a crisis, it should communicate what is known, what is not known, what is being done, what people should do and when the next update will come. After the acute phase, communication supports explanation, accountability, learning and long-term relations. Principles under pressure Speed, clarity, openness and responsibility are practical demands, not slogans. Speed without verification can cause harm. Openness has legal and ethical limits. Clarity must not conceal uncertainty. Responsibility requires visible decisions, correction and follow-up, not merely a visible spokesperson. Media, news criteria and framing News values help explain attention, not social importance. Significance, identification, sensation, timeliness, conflict, elite actors, proximity and exclusivity shape selection. Hernes’s media distortion and framing theory help analyse how crisis coverage sharpens, simplifies, personalises and attributes responsibility. Organisations cannot control this process through message discipline alone. Plans, stakeholders and alternative channels A crisis communication plan should connect principles with roles, mobilisation, situational awareness, internal communication, external communication, monitoring, technology, templates and evaluation. Alternative channels are required for loss of power, networks and internal systems. Plans must account for language, disability, unequal access and the needs of directly affected groups. Exercises and learning Exercises should test incomplete information, media pressure, internal needs, affected stakeholders, social media traffic, inter-organisational coordination and technological failure. text: Academic writing | MMP311 Skip to main content MMP311 A− A A+ Learning path Risk society Risk communication Issues management PRK and SOFT FIVER Crisis communication Academic writing 9 March, 13:15–15:15 Academic writing MMP311 · Version 1.1 · Revised 19th of November, 2026 by Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) Learning outcomes Formulate a question that the material can answer. Distinguish material, method, analysis and discussion. Use theory as an analytical tool rather than decoration. Separate documentation, interpretation and uncertainty. Use sources and AI in an auditable way. Academic writing makes the analytical movement visible. A strong text connects a precise question, defined material, a transparent method, concepts that change what can be seen, and conclusions that do not exceed the evidence. Begin with a question the material can answer A research question should identify the phenomenon, the analytical purpose and an empirical boundary. “How do Norwegian authorities communicate risk?” is too broad. “How is uncertainty framed in two public preparedness campaigns published between 2024 and 2026?” identifies both material and analytical focus. Three useful forms Theoretical essay Develop and test a conceptual argument through precise engagement with research. The essay still needs a question, an explicit selection of literature and a bounded conclusion. Case analysis Define the case, material and method. Use PRK, SOFT or FIVER only when the framework changes what the analysis can identify. A model is not evidence. Evaluation of communication practice State criteria before assessing performance. Separate what the communication contains, how it can reasonably be interpreted and what cannot be concluded without audience or outcome data. Move from evidence to interpretation A useful paragraph establishes a claim, presents observable evidence, explains the relationship and ends with a bounded interpretation. Quotations, screenshots, documents and examples must demonstrate the claim rather than decorate the text. Make theory do analytical work Define the concept, identify the relevant feature in the material, explain how the concept changes the interpretation, and state the limit of the inference. If a theory can be removed without changing the analysis, it is not doing analytical work. Distinguish material, method, analysis and discussion The material is what is studied. The method explains how it is selected and analysed. The analysis shows patterns and examples. The discussion relates findings to theory, previous research and alternative explanations. These functions may appear in different structures; IMRaD is not mandatory for every assignment. Use generative AI without outsourcing responsibility AI can support outlining, language revision and comparison of formulations. The student remains responsible for source retrieval, quotation accuracy, references, analytical decisions and the submitted text. Never cite a source that has not been opened and checked. Document AI use according to the course and institutional rules. Worked example Observation: A preparedness campaign repeatedly uses household images and imperative verbs. Evidence: Three posts show stored water, batteries and food alongside “You must be prepared”. Explanation: SOFT directs attention to framing and unequal household capacity. Interpretation: The campaign individualises preparedness, but the material alone cannot establish how audiences respond. Paraphras

text: PRK: Problem, Risk and Crisis | MMP311 Skip to main content V MMP311 Analytical framework · PRK Problem, risk and crisis PRK follows how contested problems, risk assessments and crisis conditions can develop into one another. The movement is circular rather than inevitable or linear. Use PRK in a case Compare the models What PRK helps you see Problem An organisational problem becomes visible when conduct, expectations or interpretations no longer align. Different stakeholders may disagree about both the problem and the appropriate response. Risk The issue represents risk when possible developments threaten people, values, operations, legitimacy or relationships. Assessment must include uncertainty and vulnerability, not only probability. Crisis A crisis places operations, decision-making or legitimacy under acute pressure. Crisis response can also expose older problems and produce new expectations. Problem Contested expectations and interpretations → Risk Possible harm, uncertainty and vulnerability → Crisis Acute pressure on operations or legitimacy Feedback: Crisis response and evaluation may reveal new problems and risks. Figure 1. The PRK framework. Problems, risks and crises can develop into one another; the movement is not necessarily linear. The accompanying text provides the full explanation. Use PRK in a case 01 Describe the matter What has happened, who is affected, and which expectations appear to be broken? 02 Locate the problem Is the core problem operational, organisational, communicative, political, or a combination? 03 Assess development Which values are at stake, what is uncertain, and what could make the situation more serious? 04 Consider crisis pressure Could established capacity, authority, trust or coordination become insufficient? 05 Feed learning back What must change in decisions, resources, routines or preparedness? Open the SOFT approach → Organise the work with FIVER Turn the analysis into a recurring process from understanding and identification to revision and response. Open the FIVER model → Full teaching text Working strategically and tactically with PRK PRK separates strategic analysis from tactical communication while connecting problems, risks and crises across time. Before a crisis, organisations must work with emerging problems and possible risks. During a crisis, they must manage the underlying problem, changing risks and acute crisis communication at the same time. After the acute phase, unresolved problems may create new risks and secondary crises. Strategic level: Problem Organisations must continually scan their surroundings for matters that may become contested. The first task is to establish whether anyone experiences the matter as a problem. This provides the basis for identifying stakeholders, expectations and competing interpretations. Only then can the organisation assess whether the matter represents a risk and what forms of intervention may be required. Strategic work requires openness to weak signals and perspectives outside the organisation. No organisation operates in a vacuum. Unknown or neglected factors can become visible during an acute event and may develop into a secondary crisis. text: SOFT Analytical Lens | MMP311 Skip to main content V MMP311 Analytical approach · SOFT Look beyond the risk matrix SOFT widens risk assessment by asking how social conditions, opinions, framing, transparency and organisational conditions shape what becomes visible and actionable. Use the SOFT questions Compare the models Four connected fields of attention Social conditions Who is exposed, excluded or dependent on the organisation? Consider unequal resources, language, access, vulnerability and local relationships. Opinions and expectations What do stakeholders expect, and where do expectations conflict? Public reaction is not a substitute for evidence, but it can reveal contested values. Framing Which interpretation dominates? Frames select causes, consequences, responsibility and possible solutions while other perspectives remain less visible. Transparency and organisational conditions What can the organisation know, share and change? Examine information flow, authority, culture, resources and willingness to correct the initial understanding. Social conditions Exposure, access and vulnerability Opinions Expectations, values and disagreement Framing Causes, responsibility and solutions Transparency Information, uncertainty and limits Organisational conditions Authority, culture, resources and capacity to change Figure 1. The SOFT analytical lens. The five fields supplement technical risk assessment; they do not replace it. The accompanying text defines each field. Questions for analysis Whose situation? Which groups carry the consequences, and which voices are missing from the organisation's picture? Whose expectations? What do different stakeholders consider reasonable, legitimate or safe? Whose frame? How do language, images, sources and categories define the matter? Which capacity? Can the organisation listen, coordinate, explain uncertainty and change established practice? Connect SOFT to the wider process Place the matter with PRK Use PRK to examine movement between a contested problem, risk and crisis. Open the PRK framework → Turn insight into work with FIVER Use FIVER to revise the situation analysis and organise an accountable response. Open the FIVER model → Full teaching text SOFT as a critical analytical lens Technical risk assessment cannot by itself explain how an issue becomes socially important. SOFT supplements probability and consequence analysis by examining social conditions, opinions, framing, transparency and organisational conditions. Social conditions Analysis starts with the conditions under which people encounter the issue. Exposure, resources, language, access, dependency and vulnerability are unevenly distributed. The same event may therefore have very different consequences for different groups. Opinions and expectations Stakeholder opinions are not substitutes for evidence. They can, however, reveal contested values, unmet expectations and emerging conflicts. Organisations must distinguish between disagreement about facts, disagreement about values and disagreement about what constitutes a legitimate response. Framing Frames select aspects of a matter and connect them to causes, consequences, responsibility and possible solutions. Analysis must ask which frame dominates, whose knowledge supports it and which alternatives remain less visible.
